title: US Court Revokes Citizenship of India-Born Man Who Concealed Deportation History
excerpt: A federal judge stripped Gurdev Singh Sohal of his U.S. citizenship after finding he used a false identity to naturalize in 2005, hiding a 1994 deportation order — part of a broader government push that has increased denaturalization referrals from 11 per year to 100-200 per month.
body:
• A federal judge revoked the U.S. citizenship of India-born Gurdev Singh Sohal on April 13, 2026, after finding he concealed a 1994 deportation order and used a false identity to naturalize in 2005.
  • The fraud was uncovered through the Historic Fingerprint Enrollment project, which matched digitized fingerprints from a 30-year-old deportation file to his naturalization records.
  • The Justice Department has dramatically escalated denaturalization efforts, increasing referral targets from roughly 11 cases per year to 100-200 per month for fiscal year 2026.
  • The case raises concerns for Indian-origin immigrants about the government's expanding ability to revisit decades-old immigration records.

How a 1994 Deportation Order Unraveled a Citizenship Grant

A federal court in April revoked the U.S. citizenship of Gurdev Singh Sohal, an India-born man who had been living as an American citizen for more than two decades. The ruling, issued on April 13, 2026, found that Sohal obtained his naturalization through identity fraud and by concealing a prior deportation order, according to a Department of Justice press release.

Sohal, who also used the names Dev Singh and Boota Singh Sundu, was ordered deported in 1994 under the identity "Dev Singh." Instead of leaving the United States, he assumed a fictitious identity with a different name, date of birth, and date of entry, according to the DOJ. He later became a lawful permanent resident and naturalized as a U.S. citizen in 2005 without disclosing his prior immigration history.

"If you lie to the government or hide your identity so that you can naturalize, this Administration will find you and strip you of your fraudulently acquired U.S. citizenship."

— Brett A. Shumate, Assistant Attorney General, DOJ Civil Division

Fingerprint Technology Cracked the Case

The fraud came to light in February 2020 through the Historic Fingerprint Enrollment project, a joint initiative between the Department of Justice and the Department of Homeland Security's U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services. Forensic analysts matched fingerprints tied to the 1994 deportation record with those in Sohal's 2005 naturalization file, according to the DOJ.

The match was only possible after DHS digitized paper fingerprint submission documents from older immigration files. The case illustrates how the government's digitization of legacy records has expanded its ability to revisit immigration histories that appeared settled decades earlier, according to VisaVerge.

The DOJ filed a civil denaturalization complaint against Sohal on September 24, 2025, marking it as the ninth such action since January 20, 2025. The complaint alleged three counts: that Sohal illegally procured citizenship because he was never lawfully admitted for permanent residence, that his lies prevented him from demonstrating the required good moral character, and that he procured naturalization through concealment and willful misrepresentation, according to the DOJ.

A Dramatic Escalation in Denaturalization Efforts

Sohal's case sits within a much larger enforcement push. Internal USCIS guidance issued in December 2025 directed field offices to send 100 to 200 denaturalization referrals per month to the Justice Department for fiscal year 2026, according to VisaVerge. That represents a dramatic increase from the historical average of roughly 11 cases per year.

As of June 2025, the Justice Department had formally designated denaturalization as a top-five enforcement priority. The administration's broader campaign has targeted 17 U.S. citizens in a single push, including people accused of immigration fraud, violent crimes, and identity-related offenses, according to reports.

The renewed emphasis follows the model of Operation Janus, a DHS probe that identified 315,000 cases in which fingerprints were missing from centralized databases. That effort led to the first major Indian-origin denaturalization case in 2018 involving Baljinder Singh, according to VisaVerge.

What This Means for the Indian Diaspora

The legal consequences of denaturalization can be immediate and severe. Once a court cancels citizenship, a person's status typically reverts to that of a lawful permanent resident, unless the underlying fraud leaves no lawful status to return to. In Sohal's case, the 1994 deportation order can be reinstated, according to legal experts cited by VisaVerge.

Indian-origin individuals who lose U.S. citizenship may also face risks tied to their Overseas Citizen of India status, which often depends on the legal validity of foreign citizenship. Some denaturalized individuals can face technical statelessness if their earlier Indian citizenship was renounced and cannot be easily reclaimed, according to IndiaWest.

The government has framed the campaign in narrow legal terms, focusing specifically on fraud in the naturalization process rather than targeting naturalized Americans broadly. However, the sharp increase in monthly referral targets signals that decades-old immigration records are now subject to review at a scale not seen before in American immigration enforcement.
nri_angle: The case highlights the U.S. government's expanding ability to revisit decades-old immigration records, raising concerns among Indian-origin naturalized citizens about the security of their status.
